title: Did Charles Darwin invent the office chair?

qwen_instruct.narrator: Punchy, amused storyteller, fast and confident.
qwen_instruct.darwin: Delighted, posh old-fashioned English gentleman, pleased with himself.

lines.text: Charles Darwin explained evolution. He also helped evolve your office chair.
In eighteen forty-two, Darwin moved to a quiet house in Kent, and filled his study with specimens.
Beetles. Pickled creatures. And barnacles. He spent eight years studying barnacles.
Every jar meant getting up, walking over, and sitting back down. Again and again.
So he put wheels on his armchair, and scooted from specimen to specimen.
So did Darwin invent the office chair? Not quite. Furniture had little wheels long before him.
In eighteen fifty-one, at the Great Exhibition, an American showed off a chair that swivelled, tilted, bounced on springs, and rolled.
Critics weren't impressed. It was too comfortable to be proper.

lines.speaker: critic
lines.text: A man might fall asleep in it!
Comfort won. Offices filled up with rolling, spinning chairs.
So next time you scoot across the office, remember: Darwin got there first.

experiment.notes: First video in the clean office-toon look (outlined toon sets, flat face-to-camera characters). Three sets: modern office, Darwin's study at Down House, the 1851 Great Exhibition.

facts.claim: Darwin's study at Down House holds his mahogany armchair on castors; he wrote On the Origin of Species there.
Darwin added castors to a William IV armchair in the early 1840s so he could reach his specimens while writing.
The study held preserved specimens in spirit and 'Darwin's wheeled chair'.
Darwin moved to Down House in Kent in 1842.
Darwin studied barnacles for about eight years (1846-1854).
Castors were already common on Georgian furniture before Darwin.
Thomas E. Warren's Centripetal Spring Armchair (1849) swivelled, tilted on springs and rolled on castors; shown at the 1851 Great Exhibition in London.
It sold poorly outside the US after the exhibition, deemed too comfortable for a proper office.
